lesson.title: One Pole, One Slope: Inside the First-Order Filter
lesson.summary: A first-order filter contains exactly one energy-storing element, its behavior is governed by a single time constant, and its stopband attenuation grows at a fixed, predictable rate of 20 dB per decade.
lesson.body:
Every filter you have met so far built from a single R and single C, the pattern used in RC Low-Pass Filter and in the high-pass circuit from High-Pass Filter, shares a structural feature: exactly one component stores energy, the capacitor, and the circuit's behavior is described by a first-order differential equation, the same class of circuit covered in First-Order Circuits. That single energy-storing element is what makes it a first-order filter, and its transfer function has exactly one pole, one frequency-dependent term in the denominator.

The practical consequence of having only one pole is that far from the cutoff frequency, the filter's magnitude response falls off, or for a high-pass filter rises, in direct proportion to frequency, one power of f, no more. In the language of decibels, that fixed proportionality translates into a fixed slope on a log-log plot: attenuation grows by exactly 20 dB for every tenfold, decade, increase in frequency past cutoff. This 20 dB per decade figure is not a rule of thumb, it falls directly out of the math, and every genuine first-order filter obeys it in the region well away from fc.

Take a first-order low-pass filter with fc = 1 kHz, and evaluate its response one decade above cutoff, at f = 10 kHz. The magnitude is |H(f)| = 1/√(1 + (f/fc)²) = 1/√(1 + 10²) = 1/√101 = 1/10.05, about 0.0995. In decibels, that is 20 log10(0.0995), about minus 20.04 dB. Compare that to the predicted 20 dB per decade: the match is essentially exact, off by only 0.04 dB, the small correction from the plus 1 term in the formula becoming negligible once you are a full decade past cutoff.

You will see in Filter Order and Roll-Off Rate that this 20 dB per decade is really 20 dB per decade per pole, and that adding a second energy-storing element to get a Second-Order Filter doubles that rate.
